name: Canthopexy

card.summary: Lower-lid tendon tightening without cutting the corner; well-established in blepharoplasty, unproven as an eye-shape tool.
card.note: Published evidence concerns lid support in surgical patients; looksmaxxing durability claims are untested.

quick.overview:
Canthopexy anchors the lateral canthal tendon to lift and support the lower eyelid without cutting the lid margin. Surgeons use it with lower blepharoplasty to limit lid malposition.

Looksmaxxers discuss it for canthal tilt and almond eye shape, usually as an alternative to canthoplasty.
quick.mechanism: A suture secures the lateral canthal tendon to the orbital rim, giving the lower lid support and a slight lateral lift. Canthoplasty differs by cutting the canthus.
quick.risks: Surgical papers connect lower lid surgery with lid malposition and use canthal support to reduce that risk; ectropion prevention is itself a studied use. Forum members disagree about how long results last.

lead: Canthopexy is a surgical procedure that tightens or repositions the lower eyelid by anchoring the lateral canthal tendon at the outer corner of the eye, without cutting the eyelid margin. Surgical papers present it as a routine companion to lower blepharoplasty that restores lid tone and contour and reduces the chance of lower lid malposition [1][2][14].

For appearance, the draw is the outer eye corner and lower lid position. Cosmetic surgery clinics describe candidates as people with a downward-sloping outer corner, looseness of the outer lower lid, a wish for a more almond-shaped eye, or asymmetry between the two corners [17]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to improve canthal tilt and eye shape, often under the labels almond eye or fox eye, and is compared with canthoplasty [4][5].

The published research is mainly surgical: a 1993 paper argued canthopexy should be a routine part of or alternative to lower lid blepharoplasty [1], and a 10-year review of lower blepharoplasty with routine lateral canthal support reported on outcomes with that approach [3]. Studies of canthopexy performed specifically for canthal tilt in people seeking appearance change have not been published.

chain: Suture anchors the lateral canthal tendon to the orbital rim
Lower lid is supported and lifted slightly at the outer corner
More upward-slanting, almond-shaped eye and steadier lid position
angle.text: Surgeons use canthopexy to support and lift the lower eyelid, and people interested in eye shape pursue it for a more upward-tilted outer corner and tighter lower lid line.

infobox: Canthoplasty, which divides and reattaches the tendon [17]
Support during lower blepharoplasty; ectropion prevention [1][9]
Better canthal tilt, almond or fox eye shape
Local anaesthesia, outpatient; about 30 to 60 minutes per procedure per one clinic [17]
Light activity in days; swelling settles over one to two weeks per one clinic [17]

paras: Wikipedia defines canthoplasty as plastic surgery of the medial and/or lateral canthus and says it is used in cosmetic procedures and in procedures addressing eyelid function or malposition; it does not mention canthopexy by name [6]. The canthus is the corner where the upper and lower lids meet, and the line between the two outer corners marks the upper boundary of the midface [6]. Surgical authors distinguish canthopexy, a suture-based support, from canthoplasty, which involves cutting the canthus [7]. A cosmetic clinic describes canthopexy as tightening the existing canthal tendon without detaching it and canthoplasty as detaching, reshaping and reattaching it at a new position for a larger lift [17].

A 2015 review of aesthetic canthal suspension lists three main options: canthopexy, which it calls the most conservative and which supports the lower lid over either the short or the long term; the orbicularis sling, which avoids the lateral canthus but may not suit patients with a history of dry eye; and a modified canthoplasty, generally reserved for more marked laxity, which is less common in patients seeking aesthetic blepharoplasty [14]. An algorithm for choosing between them was published in 1999, including a simplified suture canthopexy called the lateral retinacular suspension [7].

Anatomical work describes the ligamentous attachments of the lower lid and lateral canthus, which form the basis for these procedures [8]. Dissection of six fresh cadavers with histologic support mapped the deep attachments of the orbicularis oculi of the lower lid and lateral canthus, which surgeons had long recognised in canthopexy surgery but had not formally defined [8].

Transcutaneous lower blepharoplasty, in which skin is trimmed through an incision just below the lashes, has been associated with an increased risk of lower lid malposition, and routine lateral canthal support has been advocated to reduce this [3][13]. Wikipedia's blepharoplasty article states that canthopexy and canthoplasty support the lateral canthus, help maintain eyelid position and may reduce the risk of postoperative malposition [13]. The 2015 review describes canthal suspension as a tool for preventing complications in eyelids with increased laxity, relatively prominent globes or a negative vector at the eyelid-cheek junction [14].

A 1993 paper argued that canthopexy restores tone and youthful contour to the eye and can reduce the need to remove skin that appears in excess only because the lid has dropped [1]. A 2000 study reported a lateral transorbital canthopexy with a grading system for correction and prevention of ectropion, an outward-turning lower lid [9]. After facial trauma, a randomised trial studied how different subciliary approaches affect lower eyelid position after infraorbital rim fracture surgery, since scleral show, ectropion, entropion and canthal malposition are the common complications [19]. A registered trial (NCT07775417) compares two ectropion-prevention measures in orbital fracture surgery and has not yet started recruiting [11].

Cosmetic surgery practices offer canthopexy and canthoplasty to people who want a more almond-shaped eye or a corrected downward-sloping outer corner, and describe the procedures as outpatient surgery under local anaesthesia [17]. The surgeons writing on midface rejuvenation note that small adjustments in this area can produce relatively large changes in the shape and appearance of the lower lids [14][16].

One plastic surgeon's public question-and-answer page states that lateral canthopexy alone is not enough to correct scleral show, the visible white below the iris, when the underlying cause is a lack of support from the infraorbital rim or a short lower-lid layer, and that the suture-based result for that use is short-lived; the same page presents the suture technique as reversible in the short term [18].

Published variants include the lateral retinacular suspension, a simplified suture canthopexy [7]; a lateral transorbital canthopexy [9]; and lateral canthal anchoring, described in a 2003 paper [10]. Reviews of lower blepharoplasty note that the choice of transconjunctival or transcutaneous approach depends on whether skin excess is present, and that current practice also repositions orbital fat to correct inferior orbital hollowing and the lid-cheek junction [15]. An overview of lower lid laxity management is available in an oral and maxillofacial surgery atlas [20].

The midface literature adds a caution: the extent of lift achievable with midface elevation is limited, and excessive elevation can produce vertical shortening of the lower lid, round-eye deformity and ectropion; canthopexy or canthoplasty is described as protecting the repair from downward traction as it heals [16]. A 2025 review describes the pinch blepharoplasty as a lower-lid rejuvenation approach that aims to preserve lid posture [21].
On looksmax.org, members also discuss a thread titled as a non-surgical canthopexy technique [25]; no published study of non-surgical canthopexy appears in the surgical literature cited here.

Published studies are mainly surgical case series and anatomical work. They include a 10-year review of lower blepharoplasty with routine lateral canthal support [3], a paper on the lateral transorbital canthopexy for correction and prevention of ectropion with a grading system and outcome study [9], and a paper on lateral canthal anchoring [10]. A single-surgeon review of 892 blepharoplasty cases examined dry eye symptoms and chemosis afterwards, one of the other recognised effects of lid surgery [22]. No study found tests canthopexy for improving canthal tilt in people seeking appearance change.

Cosmetic clinic information lists potential complications of canthopexy and canthoplasty as bleeding or hematoma, infection, scarring, asymmetry, over- or under-correction (the latter possibly needing revision), changes in sensation, altered tear drainage or dry eye, and gradual recurrence of laxity as tissue ages [17]. The same clinic describes swelling, bruising, tightness, tearing changes and light sensitivity as common early on, with sutures usually removed within a week, swelling subsiding within one to two weeks and full healing taking several weeks [17].
Surgical papers connect lower lid surgery with lid malposition, the problem canthal support is used to reduce [3][14]. Wikipedia's canthoplasty article does not cover complications [6].

On looksmax.org, threads ask whether to choose canthopexy or canthoplasty for canthal tilt, noting conflicting online advice that canthoplasty is for people over 30 [4]. One member argues canthopexy is preferable, particularly under 40, because it does not cut the lower eyelid, while another says it may relax after a year or two [5]. A thread title argues for canthopexy rather than canthoplasty for people under 40 [23]. Others ask whether pulling the lateral corner adds millimeters of positive fixed lid length [12].

Other threads ask for before-and-after photos of infraorbital and malar canthopexy [24], ask for first-hand experiences of canthoplasty, canthopexy and infraorbital implants [26], weigh canthopexy against starting a hormone cycle [27], and discuss a posted result in relation to a named surgeon's work [28]. The discussion links canthopexy with other midface and eye-area changes such as infraorbital implants and orbital work.

timeline.event: Karl Ferdinand von Gräfe coins the term blepharoplasty while repairing eyelid deformities [13].
A paper argues canthopexy should be a routine part of or alternative to lower lid blepharoplasty [1].
An algorithm for canthoplasty and the lateral retinacular suspension, a simplified suture canthopexy, is published [7].
Lateral transorbital canthopexy for ectropion correction and prevention is reported with a grading system [9].
Cadaver study maps the ligamentous attachments of the lower lid and lateral canthus [8].
A paper on lateral canthal anchoring is published [10].
A 10-year review reports on lower blepharoplasty with routine lateral canthal support [3].
A review of aesthetic canthal suspension compares canthopexy, orbicularis sling and canthoplasty [14].
A randomised trial examines subciliary approaches and lower eyelid position after infraorbital rim fracture surgery [19].
Trial NCT07775417 on ectropion prevention in orbital fracture surgery is registered, listed as not yet recruiting [11].

lore.intro: Canthopexy is discussed on looksmax.org as a milder alternative to canthoplasty for eye shape and canthal tilt [4][5].

claims.claim: Canthopexy gives a better almond or fox eye than canthoplasty.
claims.believers: A member says canthopexy does not cut the lower eyelid and can lift and stretch the lid, and that paired with a temporal or cheek lift the result is permanent [5].
claims.experts: Surgical literature presents canthopexy as the most conservative lid support option, used during blepharoplasty and for ectropion prevention [1][9][14]. No study found tests permanence or eye-shape change for appearance goals.

claims.claim: Canthopexy results relax back within a year or two.
claims.believers: A reply in the same thread says it is weak and the eyelid returns to its original state after a year or two [5].
claims.experts: Published papers report outcomes of specific canthopexy techniques in surgical patients [3][9]; none found compares durability for cosmetic canthal tilt. One surgeon's public page says the suture-based result is short-lived when used to correct scleral show [18].

claims.claim: Canthoplasty is for people over 30; younger people should choose canthopexy.
claims.believers: A poster notes conflicting online advice and asks which to choose; another thread is titled as arguing for canthopexy under 40 [4][23].
claims.experts: A 2015 review says canthoplasty is generally reserved for more marked laxity, which is less common in aesthetic blepharoplasty patients, and that canthopexy is the most conservative option [14].

claims.claim: Pulling the lateral corner adds millimeters of positive fixed lid length.
claims.believers: A member asks whether canthopexy adds millimeters of lid length by pulling the outer corner [12].
claims.experts: Midface research notes that adjustments in this area can cause large changes in lid shape and that overcorrection can cause shortening or round-eye deformity [14][16]. No study found measures fixed lid length after cosmetic canthopexy.

claims.believers: A member says canthopexy fixes a slight scleral show and lifts the lower lid [5].
claims.experts: One plastic surgeon states that canthopexy alone is never enough to correct scleral show and that rim augmentation or a lid graft may be needed; canthal suspension is described in reviews as a complication-prevention tool for lids with laxity or negative vector [14][18].

claims.claim: Canthopexy is low-risk because the lid margin is not cut.
claims.believers: A member says canthopexy does not cut the lower eyelid, unlike canthoplasty [5].
claims.experts: A clinic lists bleeding, infection, asymmetry, over- or under-correction, dry eye and recurrence among possible complications of the two procedures [17].
